CARES Threat Model

Scope: proposed multi-tenant CARES SaaS and future self-hosted deployment, including Dashboard, API, agents, integrations, PostgreSQL, processing workers, AI provider traffic, and administrative workflows. This is a design threat model, not a penetration test or security assessment.

Assets

  • Tenant security events, asset inventory, alerts, incidents, vulnerability findings, evidence, and reports.
  • User identities, tenant memberships, agent/integration credentials, AI provider API keys, signing keys, and database credentials.
  • Licensing entitlements and usage history.
  • Detection rules, configurations, response workflows, audit records, and platform integrity.
  • Availability and integrity of ingestion, processing, and customer operations.

Actors and assumptions

Actors include customer users, CARES platform administrators, compromised endpoints/agents, malicious or misconfigured integrations, external AI providers, internet attackers, insiders, and compromised dependencies. Assume submitted logs, event fields, hostnames, file names, commands, webhook bodies, and model outputs are untrusted. Assume the hosting environment, identity provider, database, and external services can fail; their controls need verification rather than assumption.

Trust boundaries

  1. Customer browsers and networks to public CARES edge.
  2. Agents and integrations to ingestion endpoints.
  3. API and workers to PostgreSQL and secret manager.
  4. One tenant's data to another tenant's data.
  5. Customer administrators to platform operators.
  6. CARES to each explicitly selected AI SaaS endpoint.
  7. Build/release pipeline to installed server and agent artifacts.

STRIDE analysis

Threat Example Proposed controls / evidence required
Spoofing Forged tenant identity, stolen agent credential, fake webhook OIDC validation and server-side membership; unique, rotated agent credentials; signed webhooks; enrollment replay tests
Tampering Altered event, agent command, package, license counter, or audit trail TLS, signatures, schema validation, idempotency, DB constraints/transactions, protected audit sink, signed artifacts
Repudiation Admin denies viewing a customer's incident; user denies export Append-oriented audit records with actor/tenant/reason/outcome, protected retention, clock and correlation controls
Information disclosure Customer A queries B; AI provider receives restricted data; credentials leak in logs Service authorization + RLS, per-tenant relationships, privacy gate, data minimization, secret manager, redaction tests, export controls
Denial of service Ingestion flood, decompression bomb, expensive search, provider cost abuse Request/body/rate limits, bounded parser and worker queues, tenant technical quotas, timeouts, AI budgets, backpressure and load tests
Elevation of privilege Customer forges role; model tool call bypasses approval; admin has unbounded access Trusted membership, deny-by-default RBAC/ABAC, tool checks independent of model, JIT support grants, approval and audit

Priority scenarios and acceptance tests

Cross-tenant data access (critical)

Path: customer manipulates tenant IDs, resource IDs, filters, exports, background job arguments, or AI tool inputs to retrieve another tenant's data.

Required defenses: resolve tenant from authenticated membership, enforce tenant scope in every service path, enforce database RLS with a non-owner runtime role, scope relationships/foreign keys, test connection-pool reset behavior, and ensure support access is separately granted/audited.

Acceptance evidence: automated tests attempt cross-tenant reads/writes through every API/resource family, direct repository/service access under the runtime DB role, exports, asynchronous jobs, and AI tools. Any unexpected result blocks release. The current code has no persistence or API to test these controls.

Asset identity manipulation and quota bypass (high)

Path: attacker changes identity values to create duplicates, reuses another device's identity, sends concurrent enrollments, or exploits device removal/re-enrollment to evade quotas.

Required defenses: tenant-scoped canonical identity aliases with namespace, provenance, confidence class, source authentication, deterministic exact authoritative matching, atomic resolution and quota reservation, uniqueness constraints, idempotency, audited merge/split, and explicit removal/quota-release rules. IP and hostname are weak observations and cannot cause automatic merge. Ambiguous sources remain pending authorized review rather than being silently assigned.

Acceptance evidence: PostgreSQL concurrency tests at quota boundary; retries; conflicting identifiers; same device across source types; two devices with identical IP/hostname; identity claim/key rotation; lifecycle/re-enrollment; merge/split; DB restore and counter reconciliation. The current local test covers only repeated identical identity strings sequentially.

Prompt injection and AI data disclosure (high)

Path: attacker embeds instructions or sensitive fields in logs/files; user asks MELIRA to analyze them; context is transmitted or tool output exceeds permission.

Required defenses: per-call tenant/tool authorization, customer consent, classification and transmission policy enforced before provider request, evidence minimization/redaction, explicit provider/model/region selection, validated provider retention/training/data-use terms, secret-manager credentials, outbound endpoint restrictions, usage/cost budgets, untrusted-content isolation, output validation, and human approval for consequential actions. No local inference or provider failover.

Acceptance evidence: capture/mock provider transport and assert zero calls when disabled, unselected, consent absent, policy denied, region/terms unknown, or quota exceeded; test redaction/minimization across IPv4/IPv6, hostnames, usernames, secrets, nested and malformed content; prove provider A/region is not used when B is selected; test prompt injection cannot execute tools; provider outage leaves non-AI operations available. The current code makes no external request; its redaction method is not suitable as a privacy control.

AI endpoint compromise and SSRF (high)

Path: a customer configures a malicious compatible endpoint, a DNS answer changes after validation, or a redirect targets a CARES/cloud metadata/private service. Provider credentials or internal network access may be exposed.

Required defenses: provider/region endpoint allow-lists; HTTPS-only; reject userinfo and unexpected ports; validate DNS results at connection time; reject private, loopback, link-local, multicast, and metadata ranges; disable or revalidate redirects; route through restricted egress; isolate custom endpoint approval; never embed credentials in URLs or logs.

Acceptance evidence: tests for IPv4/IPv6 private and metadata addresses, DNS rebinding, redirect chains, malformed hostnames, userinfo, non-HTTPS, unexpected port, and credential leakage. Prove the egress policy blocks destinations even if application validation is bypassed.

Credential theft or misuse (high)

Path: API key or agent certificate appears in repository, dashboard response, logs, installer, or compromised host.

Required defenses: secret manager, write-only display, per-tenant access boundaries, rotation/revocation, short-lived enrollment, certificate pinning/trust lifecycle, redacted logs, artifact scanning, and incident response.

Ingestion denial of service (high)

Path: large or deeply nested payload, high-rate tenant, parser exploit, retry storm, or many duplicate events exhausts API, database, or worker capacity.

Required defenses: bounded request size/decompression, schema depth/complexity limits, per-source and per-tenant rate/technical quotas, idempotency, bounded workers/retries, outbox-lag alarms, database capacity protections, backpressure with retryable rejection before accepting data, and load/failure testing.

Initial planning target (unapproved assumption): 25 EPS sustained and 100 EPS for five minutes, up to 10 tenants/5,000 active assets, with a 1 KiB average event. These values are not measured limits or commitments. Validate on the documented reference hardware; see DATA_ARCHITECTURE.md and ADR 0005.

Privileged misuse (high)

Path: platform administrator browses customer information or changes policy without authorization or audit.

Required defenses: least privilege, JIT time/scope, reason and approval where appropriate, customer context banner, immutable/protected audit trail, alerts, periodic access review, and emergency access procedure.

Supply chain and update compromise (high)

Path: malicious dependency, build runner, package, update manifest, or agent upgrade installs code or steals credentials.

Required defenses: locked dependencies, provenance/SBOM, signed artifacts and metadata, isolated CI identities, reproducible or verifiable builds, staged rollout, signature verification by agent, and rollback.

Residual risk and validation

External AI providers receive only policy-approved data but remain external processors with their own retention, jurisdiction, and availability risks. Endpoint agents operate with elevated privileges on customer systems and are high-value targets. RLS and application checks reduce but do not eliminate risk from compromised application credentials or arbitrary SQL execution. This model must be revised when deployment, identity, data-retention, and response-action decisions are finalized. No current control should be considered verified based on this document.
